name: Tirumeninathar Temple, Tiruchuli
deity: Shiva as Tirumeninathar (Bhoominathar), with the goddess Thunaimalai Nayaki (Sahayavalli)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Pandya country, sung by Sundarar in the Tevaram (8th century); Pandya foundation with later additions
dynasty: Pandya, with later additions (boundary walls of the Setupati era)
summary: Tirumeninathar is the Shiva temple of Tiruchuli, sung by Sundarar in the Tevaram, where tradition says the Lord stilled a world-ending deluge by drawing its swirling waters into the earth, and beside which Sri Ramana Maharshi was born.

sections.history: Tiruchuli, in Virudhunagar district on the Virudhunagar-Manamadurai road, has been praised since the Tevaram as Tiruchuzhiyal. Tradition counts its temple the twelfth of the Tevaram shrines of the Pandya country, sung in the hymns of Sundarar in the seventh Tirumurai, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The original complex is believed to have been built by the Pandyas, with additions by later ruling houses, and the high boundary walls are attributed to the reign of Muthuramalinga Setupati. The name is read as the place of the swirl (chuzhi), recalling the legend of the flood. The town is honoured too as the site of a modern pilgrimage: in a house beside the temple Ramana Maharshi was born on 30 December 1879. Detailed records of the temple's foundation are scarce, so this account keeps to what tradition holds.
sections.architecture: The temple covers about two and a half acres, its shrines enclosed within concentric rectangular walls and built up over many centuries in the Dravidian manner. An elegant gopuram at the entrance leads towards the shrine of the goddess Sahayavalli, known in Tamil as Thunaimalai Nayaki. The sanctum of Tirumeninathar holds the Shiva linga, worshipped here also as Bhoominathar, the Lord of the Earth. The sacred tree is the punnai, and the temple tank has a mandapam at its centre, named Kavvaikadal in one source. Sources name the temple's sacred waters differently, and the nearby Kundaru river is among them.
sections.legends: The legend of Tiruchuli is the tale of the earth saved. At the close of an age a deluge rose to swallow the land; in one telling, in the Dwapara Yuga, the Pandya king of the region, a staunch devotee of Shiva, prayed for help. The Lord struck the ground with his trident and opened a cavity, and the floodwaters rushed into it in a great whirlpool around the trident, so that the earth, Bhoomi, was spared. From this the Lord is Bhoominathar and the place is Tiruchuzhiyal, the sacred swirl. Another telling speaks of Shiva relieving a Pandya king of a sin and bringing the deluge under control; the details differ, but the Lord who stills the waters stands at the centre of them all.
sections.festivals: The great festival is the Thirukalyanam, the divine wedding of the Lord and the goddess, held in the Tamil month of Panguni, in March or April. Chitra Pournami is also among the temple's most prominent festivals. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: A visit to Tiruchuli brings two kinds of fulfilment. Enter beneath the gopuram and come to Tirumeninathar, Lord of the Earth, and to Thunaimalai Nayaki in her own shrine, remembering the flood that was drawn down into the ground. Then walk to the house beside the temple where Ramana Maharshi was born, now a quiet memorial known as Sundara Mandiram, open to visitors for meditation. The sage of Arunachala began his life in the shadow of this sanctuary, and many pilgrims come for both. The town is small and the pace gentle.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruchuli is in Virudhunagar district on the Virudhunagar-Manamadurai road, about 15 km from Aruppukottai and roughly 55 to 60 km from Madurai. Buses connect the town with Aruppukottai, Virudhunagar and Madurai. Madurai has the nearest major railway junction and airport. The temple stands in the town, and the memorial at Ramana Maharshi's birthplace is close by.
